newsitem.title: USA: Samper accuser questioned in Miami trial.
newsitem.headline: Samper accuser questioned in Miami trial.

text.p: A star witness at a drug trial who implicated Colombian President Ernesto Samper with the Cali cocaine cartel may have himself been involved in murder conspiracies, attorneys said on Tuesday.

"The government is aware of Mr. (Guillermo) Pallomari being present at a meeting when a decision was made to retaliate against two particular people who were accused of stealing a computer from Miguel Rodriguez," said Assistant U.S. Attorney William Pearson, one of the prosecutors in the case.
Pearson was referring to Miguel Rodriguez Orejuela, who headed the infamous Colombian drug gang with his brother Gilberto.
Pallomari, a Chilean-born computer systems engineer and the prosecution's star witness, was formerly personal assistant and accountant for Miguel Rodriguez.

Defence attorneys during cross-examination of Pallomari questioned his credibility on issues including his assertions under oath that he had played purely a financial role on the cartel's "security committee," whose functions included recommending who would be added to the cartel's death list.
"Did he decide who'd be executed or not?" asked Martin Weinberg, an attorney for William Moran.
Moran, a criminal defence attorney and former federal prosecutor, was one of two U.S. lawyers on trial in U.S. District Court.

Also on trial were lawyer Michael Abbell, who was chief of the U.S. Justice Department's Office of International Affairs during the Reagan administration, and four men U.S. officials charge helped warehouse and ship drugs -- Luis Alfredo Grajales, Eddie Martinez, Ramon Martinez and Jose Luis Pereira-Salas.

Earlier in his testimony, Pallomari alleged the cartel had agents infiltrated throughout the Colombian government. Last week, he also testified that the cartel had funnelled at least $5 million into Samper's presidential campaign in 1994, charges the Colombian president has staunchly denied.

Defence attorneys have tried to present Pallomari as an untrustworthy, desperate man who has lied under oath, hopes to write a best-selling book and is willing to say anything to please U.S. prosecutors in order to avoid a lengthy prison sentence and protect the lives of his sons.
Pallomari testified on Monday that the cartel kidnapped his wife after its leaders learned he had met with U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration officials.
